plain_english: "But," says someone arguing with us, "you only practice virtue because you hope to get some pleasure from it." Let me answer that. Even if virtue does give us pleasure, that's not why we pursue her. She doesn't offer this as her main gift — it just comes along with everything else. And this isn't her goal. Her work achieves this too, but she's aiming for something else. Think of a farmer plowing his field to grow corn. He might find some flowers mixed in with the crop. Those flowers are beautiful, but he didn't do all that work just to grow them. He had another goal in mind. The flowers were just a bonus. That's how pleasure works with virtue. Pleasure isn't virtue's reward or her reason for existing — it just comes along for the ride. We don't choose virtue because she gives us pleasure. We choose virtue for other reasons, and if we do choose her, she happens to give us pleasure too.
original_excerpt: “But,” says our adversary, “you yourself only practise virtue because you hope to obtain some pleasure from it.” In the first place, even though virtue may afford us pleasure, still we do not seek after her on that account: for she does not bestow this, but bestows this to boot, nor is this the end for which she labours, but her labour wins this also, although it be directed to another end. As in a tilled-field, when ploughed for corn, some flowers are found amongst it, and yet, though these posies may charm the eye, all this labour was not spent in order to produce them—the man who sowed the field had another object in view, he gained this over and above it—so pleasure is not the reward or the cause of virtue, but comes in addition to it; nor do we choose virtue because she gives us pleasure, but she gives us pleasure also if we choose her.

plain_english:
The highest good lies in choosing virtue itself. It lies in how the noblest minds work. Once such a mind has done its job and settled within its proper bounds, it has reached the highest good. It needs nothing more. There is nothing outside the whole, just as there is nothing beyond the end.

So you are wrong when you ask me what I seek virtue for. You are looking for something higher than the highest thing. You ask what I want from virtue? The answer is: virtue herself. She has nothing better than herself. She is her own reward.

Isn't this great enough? The highest good is unshakeable strength of mind, wisdom, greatness of soul, sound judgment, freedom, harmony, and beauty. Do you still want something greater — something these qualities would just be parts of?

Why do you talk to me about pleasures? I'm trying to find what is good for human beings, not for their stomachs. Cattle and whales have bigger bellies than we do.
original_excerpt: The highest good lies in the act of choosing her, and in the attitude of the noblest minds, which when once it has fulfilled its function and established itself within its own limits has attained to the highest good, and needs nothing more: for there is nothing outside of the whole, any more than there is anything beyond the end. You are mistaken, therefore, when you ask me what it is on account of which I seek after virtue: for you are seeking for something above the highest. Do you ask what I seek from virtue? I answer. Herself: for she has nothing better; she is her own reward. Does this not appear great enough, when I tell you that the highest good is an unyielding strength of mind, wisdom, magnanimity, sound judgment, freedom, harmony, beauty? Do you still ask me for something greater, of which these may be regarded as the attributes? Why do you talk of pleasures to me? I am seeking to find what is good for man, not for his belly; why, cattle and whales have larger ones than he.
